summary: Year 4 pupils extend the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits: aligning by place value, composing (carrying) when a column total reaches ten or more, and decomposing (borrowing/exchanging) when a top digit is too small — including the hardest case, borrowing across one or more zeros (e.g. 4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking answers by rounding to estimate and by using the inverse operation, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside the exact procedure. The exchange rationale must stay explicit (a carry is 'ten of these make one of those'; a borrow is the reverse) rather than becoming a symbol-pushing trick.
misconceptions: Borrow-across-zero failure — cannot decompose when the adjacent column is 0 (4002-1367)
Smaller-from-larger bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position
Misaligns digits when the two numbers have different lengths (right-aligning wrongly, or lining up under the wrong column)
Fails to compose — leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying
Treats checking as redoing the sum rather than estimating or using the inverse

activities.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
steps: Set up 4002 - 1367 in place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers, aligning from the ones column on the right.
Build 4002 physically (or on a screen model): four thousand-blocks and two ones, with empty hundreds and tens.
Try to subtract 7 ones from 2 ones; notice there is nothing in the hundreds or tens to exchange from, so the exchange must come from the thousands.

Exchange one thousand-block into ten hundred-blocks, then one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones — watching the single thousand ripple down through the two empty columns until the ones column holds 12.
Record each changed digit in the written algorithm in step with the blocks (4002 becomes 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) and finish the subtraction to reach 2635.
Round both numbers to make an estimate (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600). Ideally do this before the exact working in the steps above. Then compare the estimate with the exact answer 2635.
activities.insight: Borrowing across zero is not a special rule: when an adjacent column is empty you continue the exchange one column further left, and a single thousand can cascade down through the zeros to free up ones. The written digits are a record of quantities actually regrouped.

activities.title: Align and compose: mixed-length columnar addition and subtraction
steps: Set out 3456 + 878 using place-value headers or grid paper, placing the 8 of 878 under the ones column (not under the left of 3456).
Add column by column; when the ones make 14, write 4 and carry one ten to the tens column rather than writing a two-digit entry in the ones.
Set out 6250 - 483, anchoring the 3 under the ones column, and subtract, exchanging from the next column left wherever the top digit is too small.
For each answer, round both numbers to estimate first, then check the exact result with the inverse operation.
activities.insight: Digits are added or subtracted by matching place value, anchored from the ones column on the right regardless of how many digits each number has; a column result of ten or more is carried, and a column that is too small to subtract requires exchanging from the next column left.

activities.title: Check it two ways: estimate and inverse
steps: After solving 4002 - 1367, round both numbers (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600) on a number line or strip and say whether 2635 is reasonable.
Check the same answer a second, independent way by adding the result to the number subtracted: 2635 + 1367 should return 4002.
Answer: 'What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead — does that change how you borrow?' and explain.
Compare the two forms of checking and say what each one catches that the other might miss.
activities.insight: Checking is not redoing the same subtraction: estimation catches place-value-scale slips, and the inverse addition independently confirms the exact answer. They are complementary, not repetition.

checkQuestion: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching how they line the digits up: 3456 + 878; 4002 - 1367; 6250 - 483. Then ask them to check the 4002 - 1367 answer two ways - by estimating and by the inverse.
checkAnswer: Aligns each sum by place value (878 under the right-hand end of 3456; 483 under the ones/tens/hundreds of 6250), composes tens/hundreds/thousands when carrying, and exchanges correctly across BOTH zeros in 4002-1367 (treating 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) to get 2635. Estimate approx 4000-1400 = 2600, close to 2635; inverse 2635+1367 = 4002.
